_comment: The Research company type (scripts/sim/research.gd). Research ships (ship_models.json research: depth_m, gear_slots) carry gear (gear: cost a share of the ship's price, which lines can fit it) and go out to sites (each site's lane end '@res_ID', laid by tools/build_map_data.gd --fishing-only), holding on station for the site's days to survey it. A site can only be researched by a ship deep enough (depth_m) with its needs fitted. Personal research earns no money: XP (xp_per_day of a same-tier cargo ship's rate x difficulty), the journal, the rating, and perks: each category's at 25/50/100% of its sites done (stat, steps) and the local ones (local_perks). Contracts come from a board shared by every company (board_size offers, new ones every refresh_days, expiring after expire_days unless taken): a site (or an oil and gas field or fishing ground for industry surveys) with a client, kind, pay (pay_rate of the price of the cheapest research ship that could do it, a day, for its days on station plus 8, x kind pay x difficulty) and deadline (deadline_days plus the trip). Failing one forfeits its pay and charges penalty x pay. Dives fail (losing a day) at fail_chance_per_day x (1.5 - maintenance); an ROV or sub can be lost on sites deeper than gear_loss_depth when maintenance is under gear_loss_maintenance (gear_loss_chance a dive). Hidden sites (famous false) show as a search area hint_nm across, off centre, until revealed: by a sonar ship working within reveal_nm, by finishing a site within reveal_nm, or by a contract.

perk.name: Catch
perk.text: {p} catch for fishing and crabbing boats

perk.name: Port fees
perk.text: {p} port fees (ports love their history told)

perk.name: Sale prices
perk.text: {p} on what every cargo sells for

gear.name: Sonar suite
gear.blurb: Multibeam and side-scan sonar: maps a site 20% faster, reveals hidden sites nearby and is needed to find wrecks and map the deeps.

gear.name: ROV
gear.blurb: A remotely operated vehicle on a tether, to the ship's depth: for wrecks, vents and anything too deep for divers.

gear.name: Crewed submersible
gear.blurb: A crewed deep submersible for the hadal deeps: needed for record dives, and half as much XP again on any dive.

gear.name: Ice hull
gear.blurb: An ice-strengthened hull for the Arctic and Antarctic sites.

gear.name: Coring rig & wet lab
gear.blurb: Corers, samplers and a wet lab aboard: needed at vents, seeps and cold-water corals and for sampling contracts.

gear.name: Dive team
gear.blurb: Divers and a recompression chamber for shallow wrecks, reefs and sunken cities (down to 60 m).

gear.name: Film crew
gear.blurb: Cameras and a crew: documentary contracts pay half as much again, and every discovery earns 10% more XP.

sites.name: Challenger Deep
sites.fact: The deepest known point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench; Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first reached it in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960.

sites.name: Sirena Deep
sites.fact: A second great deep at the eastern end of the Mariana Trench, almost as deep as the Challenger Deep.

sites.name: Horizon Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Tonga Trench and the second deepest place on Earth, named for the research ship Horizon.

sites.name: Scholl Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Kermadec Trench north of New Zealand, over ten kilometres down.

sites.name: Emden Deep
sites.fact: The bottom of the Philippine Trench, named for the German cruiser Emden whose crew first sounded it.

sites.name: Kuril-Kamchatka Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the trench running down from Kamchatka, where the Pacific plate dives under the Okhotsk plate.

sites.name: Izu-Ogasawara Trench
sites.fact: Home of the deepest fish ever filmed, a snailfish seen at 8,336 metres in 2022.

sites.name: Japan Trench
sites.fact: The trench whose great slip in 2011 set off the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami.

sites.name: Brownson Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Atlantic, at the bottom of the Puerto Rico Trench.

sites.name: Meteor Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the South Sandwich Trench, named for the German survey ship Meteor.

sites.name: Factorian Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Southern Ocean, first dived in 2019 on the Five Deeps Expedition.

sites.name: Richards Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Atacama Trench off Chile, where the Nazca plate slides under South America.

sites.name: Java Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Indian Ocean, in the Java Trench south of Bali.

sites.name: Aleutian Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the long trench curving under the Aleutian Islands.

sites.name: Molloy Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Arctic Ocean, in the Fram Strait between Greenland and Svalbard.

sites.name: Calypso Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Mediterranean, in the Hellenic Trench west of Greece.

sites.name: Bartlett Deep
sites.fact: The deepest point of the Caribbean, in the Cayman Trough between Cuba and Jamaica.

sites.name: Diamantina Deep
sites.fact: A deep scar of the Diamantina Fracture Zone, torn as Australia split from Antarctica.

sites.name: Romanche Trench
sites.fact: A great gash across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge on the equator, where Atlantic bottom water pours through.

sites.name: Planet Deep
sites.fact: The bottom of the New Britain Trench, named for the German survey ship Planet.

sites.name: Yap Trench
sites.fact: A deep, narrow trench south of the Mariana Trench, home to amphipods found nowhere else.

sites.name: Palau Trench
sites.fact: A trench east of Palau whose steep walls are some of the least explored in the Pacific.

sites.name: Ryukyu Trench
sites.fact: The trench along the Ryukyu Islands, where the Philippine Sea plate sinks beneath Japan.

sites.name: Middle America Trench
sites.fact: The trench off Mexico and Central America whose quakes have shaped the coast for millions of years.

sites.name: RMS Titanic
sites.fact: The White Star liner sank on her maiden voyage after striking an iceberg; Robert Ballard's team found her in 1985.

sites.name: Endurance
sites.fact: Shackleton's ship, crushed by the Weddell Sea ice, was found upright and astonishingly whole in 2022.

sites.name: SS Central America
sites.fact: The 'Ship of Gold' went down in a hurricane with tons of California gold.

sites.name: SS Andrea Doria
sites.fact: The Italian liner sank after a collision off Nantucket; divers call her the Mount Everest of wreck diving.

sites.name: SS Edmund Fitzgerald
sites.fact: The Great Lakes freighter broke in two in a November gale on Lake Superior with all 29 hands.

sites.name: Nuestra Senora de Atocha
sites.fact: A Spanish treasure galleon lost in a hurricane off the Florida Keys, laden with silver and emeralds.

sites.name: San Jose galleon
sites.fact: Called the holy grail of shipwrecks, this Spanish galleon sank in battle off Cartagena with a vast treasure.

sites.name: Whydah Gally
sites.fact: The only fully verified pirate shipwreck, the flagship of Black Sam Bellamy, lost off Cape Cod.

sites.name: Antikythera wreck
sites.fact: A Roman-era wreck that gave up the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient gear-driven astronomical computer.

sites.name: Batavia
sites.fact: A Dutch East Indiaman wrecked on the Houtman Abrolhos, scene of a bloody mutiny among the survivors.

sites.name: HMS Erebus
sites.fact: One of the two ships of Franklin's lost expedition to find the Northwest Passage.

sites.name: HMS Terror
sites.fact: Franklin's second ship, found in Terror Bay so well preserved that her windows were still intact.

sites.name: SS Republic
sites.fact: A Civil War-era steamer lost in a hurricane off Georgia with a cargo of coins.

sites.name: MS Zenobia
sites.fact: A ro-ro ferry that capsized off Larnaca on her maiden voyage, now one of the world's best wreck dives.

sites.name: SS Yongala
sites.fact: A passenger ship lost in a cyclone off Queensland, now teeming with rays, turtles and giant groupers.

sites.name: Esmeralda
sites.fact: A ship of Vasco da Gama's fleet wrecked off Oman, the oldest European ship of the Age of Discovery found.

sites.name: Belitung wreck
sites.fact: A Tang dynasty dhow carrying some 60,000 pieces of Chinese ceramics, proof of an early maritime silk road.

sites.name: SS Gairsoppa
sites.fact: A British cargo ship whose 110 tonnes of silver were raised from almost 5 kilometres down.

sites.name: RMS Lusitania
sites.fact: The Cunard liner was torpedoed off Ireland with the loss of 1,198 lives, helping turn opinion against Germany.

sites.name: RMS Empress of Ireland
sites.fact: The liner sank in 14 minutes after a collision in the fog on the St. Lawrence.

sites.name: Flor de la Mar
sites.fact: A Portuguese carrack lost in the Strait of Malacca with the plunder of Malacca; she has never been found.

sites.name: SS Waratah
sites.fact: A liner that vanished without a trace off South Africa with 211 aboard; searches have never found her.

sites.name: MS Estonia
sites.fact: The ferry sank in a storm in the Baltic, the deadliest peacetime sinking in modern European waters.

sites.name: RMS Rhone
sites.fact: A Royal Mail steamer wrecked in a hurricane in the British Virgin Islands, now a famous dive site.

sites.name: Mary Celeste
sites.fact: The ship found sailing with no one aboard in 1872 was later run onto a reef off Haiti, where her remains may lie.

sites.name: Lost City Hydrothermal Field
sites.fact: Towers of white carbonate up to 60 metres tall, vented by warm alkaline fluids that may resemble where life began.

sites.name: TAG hydrothermal field
sites.fact: A great mound of black smokers on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the first vent field found in the Atlantic.

sites.name: Rainbow vent field
sites.fact: Vents on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rich in hydrogen and methane, named for the colours of their plumes.

sites.name: Snake Pit
sites.fact: A black smoker field on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge carpeted with shrimp that sense the vents' glow.

sites.name: Lucky Strike
sites.fact: One of the largest vent fields known, around a lava lake on a volcano of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

sites.name: Menez Gwen
sites.fact: A shallow vent field near the Azores where mussels crowd the warm springs.

sites.name: Beebe Vent Field
sites.fact: The deepest known hydrothermal vents, in the Cayman Trough, venting fluid at over 400 degrees Celsius.

sites.name: Von Damm vent field
sites.fact: Vents on the flank of an undersea mountain in the Cayman Trough with talc chimneys and blind shrimp.

sites.name: Galapagos Rift
sites.fact: The first hydrothermal vents ever seen, with giant tube worms and clams living off chemicals instead of sunlight.

sites.name: East Pacific Rise 9N
sites.fact: One of the fastest-spreading ridges, where scientists have watched new seafloor erupt twice.

sites.name: Guaymas Basin
sites.fact: Vents in the Gulf of California that cook buried sediment into oil and feed orange microbial mats.

sites.name: Endeavour Segment
sites.fact: A ridge off Canada with chimneys taller than houses, Canada's first marine protected area.

sites.name: Champagne Vent
sites.fact: A vent near the Mariana Arc bubbling droplets of liquid carbon dioxide from the seafloor.

sites.name: Kairei Field
sites.fact: Home of the scaly-foot snail, which builds its shell and armour from iron sulfides.

sites.name: Loki's Castle
sites.fact: Black smokers on the Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge, near where the Lokiarchaeota microbes were found.

sites.name: Brine Pool, Gulf of Mexico
sites.fact: A lake of super-salty water on the seafloor so dense it has a shore, deadly to animals that swim in.

sites.name: Hydrate Ridge
sites.fact: A ridge off Oregon where methane ice burns at the touch of a flame and seeps feed clams and microbes.

sites.name: Jan Mayen vent fields
sites.fact: The Troll Wall and Soria Moria vents on the Mohns Ridge, the Arctic Ridge's white smokers, crowded with sponges and amphipods.

sites.name: East Scotia Ridge vents
sites.fact: Antarctic vents crowded with a new species of yeti crab, nicknamed the Hoff crab.

sites.name: Kolumbo volcano
sites.fact: A submarine volcano near Santorini whose crater holds vents and pools of acidic, carbon-rich water.

sites.name: Iheya North
sites.fact: Vents in the Okinawa Trough where scientists measured electricity flowing from the hot fluids.

sites.name: Brothers Volcano
sites.fact: A submarine volcano on the Kermadec Arc with vents both in its caldera and up its walls.

sites.name: Hakon Mosby mud volcano
sites.fact: A mud volcano on the Barents Sea slope, a kilometre across, bubbling methane.

sites.name: Axial Seamount
sites.fact: The most active volcano off the US west coast, wired to the shore with cables to watch its eruptions.

sites.name: Kama'ehuakanaloa Seamount
sites.fact: The young volcano off Hawaii's Big Island that will one day rise to become the next Hawaiian island.

sites.name: Bowie Seamount
sites.fact: A seamount off Haida Gwaii rising to 24 metres from the surface, crowded with rockfish.

sites.name: Tamu Massif
sites.fact: Perhaps the largest single volcano on Earth, about the size of the British Isles, buried under the Pacific.

sites.name: Ontong Java Plateau
sites.fact: The largest volcanic plateau on Earth, the size of Alaska, made in a burst of eruptions.

sites.name: Great Meteor Seamount
sites.fact: A huge flat-topped seamount south of the Azores, once an island worn flat by the waves.

sites.name: Vema Seamount
sites.fact: A seamount off Namibia whose top, 26 metres down, was home to rock lobsters till they were fished out.

sites.name: Reykjanes Ridge
sites.fact: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge running south-west from Iceland, the seam where Europe and North America part.

sites.name: Gorringe Ridge
sites.fact: A ridge off Portugal rising from 5,000 metres to 25 metres from the surface, rich with kelp and fish.

sites.name: Detroit Seamount
sites.fact: One of the oldest of the Emperor Seamounts, a 76-million-year-old trail of the Hawaiian hotspot.

sites.name: Davidson Seamount
sites.fact: A seamount off California called an oasis in the deep, with coral forests and an octopus garden.

sites.name: Cobb Seamount
sites.fact: A seamount off Washington whose summit rises to 34 metres from the surface, home to rockfish and sponges.

sites.name: Monowai
sites.fact: One of the most active submarine volcanoes, which once grew 72 metres in two weeks.

sites.name: Kick 'em Jenny
sites.fact: The most active submarine volcano of the Caribbean, north of Grenada, with an exclusion zone for ships.

sites.name: Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai
sites.fact: The 2022 eruption was the most violent ever recorded by instruments, its shock wave circling the Earth.

sites.name: Marsili Seamount
sites.fact: The largest volcano in Europe, 70 kilometres long, hidden under the Tyrrhenian Sea.

sites.name: Anaximander Mountains
sites.fact: Mountains off Turkey with mud volcanoes and methane ice on their slopes.

sites.name: Walvis Ridge
sites.fact: A ridge running from Namibia into the South Atlantic, the trail of the Tristan hotspot.

sites.name: Ninety East Ridge
sites.fact: One of the straightest features on Earth, a ridge running 5,000 kilometres north-south along 90 degrees east.

sites.name: Lord Howe Rise
sites.fact: Part of Zealandia, the drowned continent, of which New Zealand is the tip.

sites.name: Kerguelen Plateau
sites.fact: A drowned volcanic plateau three times the size of Japan, once covered in forest.

sites.name: Fieberling Guyot
sites.fact: A flat-topped seamount off California, the best studied guyot in the Pacific.

sites.name: Salas y Gomez Ridge
sites.fact: A chain of over a hundred seamounts east of Easter Island, many found and explored only in 2024.

sites.name: Rockall
sites.fact: A granite stack in the Atlantic, the tip of a drowned bank whose waters are fished hard.

sites.name: Ribbon Reefs
sites.fact: The outer wall of the Great Barrier Reef, the largest structure built by living things.

sites.name: Raja Ampat
sites.fact: The richest reef on Earth for corals and fish, at the heart of the Coral Triangle.

sites.name: Tubbataha Reefs
sites.fact: Atolls in the Sulu Sea so well protected they hold over 600 kinds of fish.

sites.name: Belize Barrier Reef
sites.fact: The second-largest barrier reef in the world, which Darwin called the most remarkable in the West Indies.

sites.name: Ras Mohammed
sites.fact: The southern tip of Sinai, where reef walls drop into the Red Sea and sharks gather in summer.

sites.name: Aldabra Atoll
sites.fact: A raised atoll in the Seychelles, home to giant tortoises and almost untouched reefs.

sites.name: Great Chagos Bank
sites.fact: The largest atoll structure in the world, in one of the cleanest seas left.

sites.name: Kingman Reef
sites.fact: A reef so untouched that sharks make up most of its fish.

sites.name: Komodo reefs
sites.fact: Strong currents around Komodo bring mantas, sharks and vivid reefs.

sites.name: Ningaloo Reef
sites.fact: A fringing reef so close to shore you can walk in, where whale sharks gather each autumn.

sites.name: Looe Key
sites.fact: A spur-and-groove reef in the Florida Keys, named for HMS Looe, wrecked on it in 1744.

sites.name: Channel Islands kelp forest
sites.fact: Forests of giant kelp off California, which can grow half a metre a day.

sites.name: Great Southern Reef
sites.fact: The kelp-forested reefs along southern Australia, home to the weedy sea dragon.

sites.name: Falklands kelp forests
sites.fact: Dense giant kelp round the Falklands, home to penguins hunting and sea lions.

sites.name: Pulley Ridge
sites.fact: The deepest light-dependent coral reef in the US, its corals grown flat to catch the dim light.

sites.name: Rost Reef
sites.fact: The largest known cold-water coral reef, built by Lophelia off the Lofoten Islands.

sites.name: Darwin Mounds
sites.fact: Hundreds of mounds of cold-water coral off Scotland, with odd 'tails' of sand.

sites.name: Sula Reef
sites.fact: A cold-water coral reef 14 kilometres long on the Norwegian shelf.

sites.name: Sipadan
sites.fact: An oceanic island off Borneo whose wall drops 600 metres, circled by turtles and barracuda.

sites.name: Rainbow Reef
sites.fact: A reef in Fiji's Somosomo Strait famous for its soft corals.

sites.name: Bonaire reefs
sites.fact: Fringing reefs round Bonaire, protected from the surface to 60 metres since 1979.

sites.name: Rowley Shoals
sites.fact: Three atolls off Western Australia that rise from deep water, untouched by rivers.

sites.name: Osprey Reef
sites.fact: A reef in the Coral Sea rising from 2,000 metres, famous for its sharks.

sites.name: Darwin's Arch
sites.fact: In the far north of the Galapagos, hammerhead sharks school in their hundreds.

sites.name: Amazon Reef
sites.fact: A reef found in 2016 under the muddy plume of the Amazon, where no one thought one could grow.

sites.name: Pavlopetri
sites.fact: The oldest known submerged town, with streets, houses and tombs laid out on the seabed off Greece.

sites.name: Thonis-Heracleion
sites.fact: Egypt's great port before Alexandria, found in Aboukir Bay with temples and giant statues.

sites.name: Canopus
sites.fact: A sunken city of temples near Thonis-Heracleion, famous in its day for its luxury.

sites.name: Port Royal
sites.fact: The pirates' 'wickedest city on Earth', two-thirds of which slid into the sea in an earthquake.

sites.name: Baiae
sites.fact: A Roman resort of villas and baths, now an underwater park with mosaics and statues.

sites.name: Alexandria's royal quarter
sites.fact: The sunken palaces of the Ptolemies and stones of the Pharos lighthouse in Alexandria's harbour.

sites.name: Dwarka
sites.fact: Stone structures off Gujarat linked to the legendary city of Krishna.

sites.name: Yonaguni Monument
sites.fact: Terraced rock off Japan; some see a sunken pyramid, most geologists natural stone.

sites.name: Atlit Yam
sites.fact: A Neolithic village off Israel with houses, wells and a circle of standing stones.

sites.name: Uluburun shipwreck
sites.fact: A Bronze Age ship with copper, tin, glass and gold from seven cultures.

sites.name: Doggerland
sites.fact: The land bridge between Britain and Europe drowned as the ice melted; trawlers still drag up mammoth bones.

sites.name: Olous
sites.fact: A Minoan and Greek city off Crete, sunk by an earthquake, whose walls show at low water.

sites.name: Phanagoria
sites.fact: The largest ancient Greek city on Russian soil, a third of it now under the Black Sea.

sites.name: Apollonia of Cyrene
sites.fact: The harbour of Cyrene in Libya, lost to an earthquake, its quays still under the sea.

sites.name: Mahabalipuram
sites.fact: Temples off southern India, glimpsed when the 2004 tsunami pulled the sea back.

sites.name: Kekova
sites.fact: A Lycian town off Turkey whose stairs and walls lead down into the sea.

sites.name: Epidaurus sunken city
sites.fact: Walls and a Roman villa under the bay of Epidaurus in Greece.

sites.name: Caesarea Maritima
sites.fact: Herod's great harbour, built with Roman concrete that set under water.

sites.name: Neapolis
sites.fact: A Roman town off Tunisia lost to a tsunami, with tanks for making fish sauce.

sites.name: Rungholt
sites.fact: A North Frisian trading town drowned in a great storm flood, found under the Wadden Sea mud.

sites.name: Dunwich
sites.fact: Once one of England's great ports, eaten away by the sea; its church bells are said to ring under the waves.

sites.name: Bimini Road
sites.fact: A line of limestone blocks off the Bahamas that some called a road to Atlantis.

sites.name: Cancun Underwater Museum
sites.fact: Hundreds of sculptures sunk off Cancun to grow into a reef and draw divers off the natural ones.

sites.name: Truk Lagoon
sites.fact: The Ghost Fleet: dozens of Japanese ships and planes sunk in Operation Hailstone, the world's greatest wreck dive.

sites.name: Scapa Flow
sites.fact: Where the German High Seas Fleet scuttled itself in 1919; seven of its ships still lie on the bottom.

sites.name: Bikini Atoll
sites.fact: The ships of the 1946 atomic bomb tests, the carrier USS Saratoga among them.

sites.name: USS Indianapolis
sites.fact: Torpedoed after delivering the atomic bomb's parts; most of her crew died in the water before rescue.

sites.name: Bismarck
sites.fact: The German battleship sank after a famous chase; Robert Ballard found her in 1989.

sites.name: HMS Hood
sites.fact: The pride of the Royal Navy, blown up by the Bismarck with only three survivors of 1,418.

sites.name: USS Arizona
sites.fact: The battleship sunk in the attack on Pearl Harbor, still leaking drops of oil today.

sites.name: IJN Yamato
sites.fact: The largest battleship ever built, sunk on a one-way mission to Okinawa.

sites.name: IJN Musashi
sites.fact: Yamato's sister ship, sunk in the Sibuyan Sea and found by Paul Allen's team in 2015.

sites.name: USS Johnston
sites.fact: The deepest shipwreck ever dived, a destroyer that charged Japanese battleships off Samar.

sites.name: SS Thistlegorm
sites.fact: A British supply ship bombed in the Red Sea, her holds still full of motorbikes, trucks and rifles.

sites.name: Wilhelm Gustloff
sites.fact: The deadliest sinking in history: some 9,000 lost when she was torpedoed carrying refugees.

sites.name: HMHS Britannic
sites.fact: Titanic's sister, sunk by a mine as a hospital ship, the largest liner on the seabed.

sites.name: USS Lexington
sites.fact: An aircraft carrier lost at the Battle of the Coral Sea, found with her planes still on the seabed.

sites.name: Akagi
sites.fact: A Japanese carrier sunk at Midway, the turning point of the Pacific war.

sites.name: USS Yorktown
sites.fact: The American carrier lost at Midway, found standing upright by Robert Ballard.

sites.name: Nikumaroro
sites.fact: The island where some think Amelia Earhart's plane came down; its reef slope has been searched for decades.

sites.name: MH370 search area
sites.fact: The vast search for the missing Malaysia Airlines flight mapped some of the least known seafloor on Earth.

sites.name: Air France 447
sites.fact: An airliner lost over the Atlantic; its recorders were recovered from almost 4 kilometres down.

sites.name: Saint-Exupery's P-38
sites.fact: The plane of the author of The Little Prince, found off Marseille.

sites.name: HMS Victoria
sites.fact: A battleship that stands vertically on the seabed, bow down, off Lebanon.

sites.name: U-869
sites.fact: A U-boat found off New Jersey by divers who spent years proving which one she was.

sites.name: Mars
sites.fact: A Swedish warship lost in battle, so well preserved in the Baltic that her cannon are still aboard.

sites.name: SMS Scharnhorst
sites.fact: The flagship of Admiral von Spee, sunk at the Battle of the Falklands.

sites.name: Great Blue Hole
sites.fact: A round sinkhole 300 metres across in a Belize atoll, made famous by Jacques Cousteau.

sites.name: Dean's Blue Hole
sites.fact: A blue hole in the Bahamas where freedivers set world records.

sites.name: Dragon Hole
sites.fact: The Sansha Yongle Blue Hole in the South China Sea, once thought the deepest blue hole.

sites.name: Taam Ja' Blue Hole
sites.fact: The deepest known blue hole, in Chetumal Bay off Mexico, so deep its bottom hasn't been reached.

sites.name: Monterey Canyon
sites.fact: A canyon as deep as the Grand Canyon just off California, studied daily by robots.

sites.name: Congo Canyon
sites.fact: The Congo River's canyon cut into the seafloor, where mud avalanches have snapped undersea cables.

sites.name: Zhemchug Canyon
sites.fact: The largest submarine canyon in the world, in the Bering Sea.

sites.name: Hudson Canyon
sites.fact: A canyon off New York with deep-sea corals and methane seeps.

sites.name: Whittard Canyon
sites.fact: A branching canyon off Ireland with vertical coral walls.

sites.name: Nazare Canyon
sites.fact: The canyon that funnels the swell into the world's biggest surfed waves at Nazare.

sites.name: Swatch of No Ground
sites.fact: A deep canyon in the Bay of Bengal, home to dolphins and Bryde's whales.

sites.name: Kaikoura Canyon
sites.fact: A canyon so close to New Zealand that sperm whales feed within sight of shore.

sites.name: Perth Canyon
sites.fact: A canyon off Perth where pygmy blue whales come to feed.

sites.name: Great Bahama Canyon
sites.fact: One of the deepest canyons on Earth, its walls 4 kilometres high.

sites.name: The Gully
sites.fact: The largest canyon off eastern North America, home to the northern bottlenose whale.

sites.name: Sac Actun caves
sites.fact: The world's longest known underwater cave, with Maya bones and Ice Age animals inside.

sites.name: Andros blue holes
sites.fact: Hundreds of blue holes round Andros, their deep water without oxygen keeping old bones and fossils.

sites.name: Gozo Blue Hole
sites.fact: A pool in the rocks of Malta leading through an arch to the open sea.

sites.name: Dahab Blue Hole
sites.fact: A blue hole in the Red Sea with an arch at 55 metres that lures divers too deep.

sites.name: Grotta Azzurra
sites.fact: A sea cave on Capri lit electric blue by sunlight through an underwater opening.

sites.name: Bloody Bay Wall
sites.fact: A wall off Little Cayman dropping from 6 metres into the deep.

sites.name: Tongue of the Ocean
sites.fact: A deep trough in the Bahama Banks, used to test submarines and sonar.

sites.name: Mississippi Canyon
sites.fact: A canyon off Louisiana cut by an ancient landslide, where oil wells now drill.

sites.name: The Bloop
sites.fact: An ultra-low sound heard across the Pacific in 1997, later thought to be ice breaking off Antarctica.

sites.name: Baltic Sea Anomaly
sites.fact: A round formation found by sonar in 2011, called a sunken UFO by some, rock by geologists.

sites.name: Bermuda Triangle
sites.fact: Where Flight 19's five bombers vanished in 1945, and legends grew of ships and planes lost.

sites.name: Ogasawara giant squid
sites.fact: The first giant squid filmed alive in its home, in the deep water off the Ogasawara Islands.

sites.name: Dominica sperm whales
sites.fact: A clan of sperm whales living year-round off Dominica, whose clicks are being decoded.

sites.name: Silver Bank
sites.fact: The humpback whales' main breeding ground in the North Atlantic.

sites.name: Dondra Head blue whales
sites.fact: Blue whales that live off Sri Lanka all year rather than migrating.

sites.name: White Shark Cafe
sites.fact: A patch of mid-Pacific where great white sharks gather each spring, nobody quite knows why.

sites.name: Sardine run
sites.fact: Shoals of sardines miles long run up South Africa's coast, chased by dolphins, sharks and gannets.

sites.name: Sodwana Bay coelacanths
sites.fact: Coelacanths, fish thought extinct for 66 million years, living in caves off South Africa.

sites.name: Comoros coelacanths
sites.fact: The home of the coelacanth, where local fishermen had long caught the fish called 'gombessa'.

sites.name: Hanifaru Bay mantas
sites.fact: A bay in the Maldives where hundreds of manta rays feed together in the monsoon.

sites.name: Lancaster Sound narwhals
sites.fact: The summer home of most of the world's narwhals.

sites.name: Antarctic krill swarms
sites.fact: Krill swarms so big they show from space, feeding the whales of the Southern Ocean.

sites.name: Tromso orcas
sites.fact: Orcas and humpbacks that follow the herring into the fjords of northern Norway.

sites.name: The Upsweep
sites.fact: A rising sound heard every season since 1991, perhaps from undersea volcanoes.

sites.name: Guanahacabibes formations
sites.fact: Stone shapes off Cuba some called a sunken city; scientists aren't convinced.

sites.name: Sargasso Sea eel spawning
sites.fact: Where European eels cross an ocean to spawn, a mystery for 2,000 years.

sites.name: Milky seas
sites.fact: Miles of sea glowing white at night with bacteria, long a sailors' tale.

sites.name: Great Pacific Garbage Patch
sites.fact: A slow gyre gathering plastic, now home to its own drifting life.

sites.name: Barents Sea craters
sites.fact: Seafloor craters blown out by methane as the ice sheet above them melted.

sites.name: Dragon's Triangle
sites.fact: The Pacific's Bermuda Triangle south of Japan, a tale of lost ships and volcanic seas.

sites.name: Red Sea brine pools
sites.fact: Pools of brine so salty they kill what swims in, keeping a record of the Red Sea's past.

sites.name: Holbox whale sharks
sites.fact: Hundreds of whale sharks gathering off Mexico to feed on tuna eggs.
